Title: The State as Ultimate Steward of Medical Autonomy for Trans Minors

Introduction
In democratic societies, medical treatment is ordinarily mediated by the triad of child, physician, and parent. Yet gender-affirming care for minors occupies a unique and urgent category, because its window for optimal efficacy is narrow while its stakes—lifelong mental health, bodily integrity, and even life itself—are unambiguously high. Accordingly, only the state—having an independent constitutional and ethical duty toward all children—is capable of securing that care when either parental prohibition threatens harm or parental permission collides with the child’s evolving, non-conforming identity. This essay advances the strong claim that legislatures and courts must possess and must exercise plenary authority to override parental decisions regarding gender-affirming healthcare for minors, regardless of whether the parents are obstructive or facilitative. The argument proceeds along four intersecting axes: children’s constitutional liberty interests, medical ethics and evidence, the state’s parens patriae power, and pragmatic rule-of-law considerations that forbid ad-hoc exemptions to universal child-welfare standards.

I. Children’s Fundamental Rights Outrank Parental Discretion

Parental rights, long a fixture of constitutional jurisprudence, are not absolute. The Supreme Court in Parham v. J.R. (1979) acknowledged the “dominant role” of parents while simultaneously recognizing that “the statist concept” must intervene to protect children when parents fall short. Prince v. Massachusetts (1944) drove the point home: “Parents may be free to become martyrs themselves, but it does not follow they are free … to make martyrs of their children.”

Gender identity is a core aspect of personhood. Numerous federal appellate and district courts have thus recognized that trans youth possess a constitutional liberty interest in accessing care necessary to preserve their health. Indeed, Yoder v. Wisconsin (1972), often cited in defense of parental authority, contains an overlooked dictum: parental rights yield when their “psychological or physical harm” to the child is imminent. Excluding a minor from puberty blockers, hormone therapy, or—in carefully regulated, late-adolescent cases—surgery, predictably results in acute distress, suicidality, and long-term bodily damage. Courts therefore have a positive obligation—enforceable via state intervention—to eject parental vetoes that abridge those rights, precisely because minors are categorically unrepresented in majoritarian politics.

II. The Medical and Ethical Consensus

Every major pediatric and psychiatric association in North America—including the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Endocrine Society, and the American Psychiatric Association—has issued evidence-based guidelines affirming that timely, developmentally staged gender-affirming care improves mental-health outcomes dramatically. An often-repeated meta-analysis spanning two decades (Turban et al., Pediatrics 2022) finds that access to puberty blockers alone reduces lifetime suicidality by roughly 40 percent. By contrast, the only peer-reviewed studies identifying “regret” or “desistance” rates capable of informing clinical decisions demonstrate vanishingly small numbers under strict gatekeeping protocols.

Parental refusal is therefore not a difference of opinion; it is active medical neglect. Yet the opposite problem also arises: parents who readily consent but whose child later expresses contrary wishes, or parents whose consent is rooted in political or social motivations external to the minor’s best interest. A minor may fear a transition she does not want, precisely because a parent insists upon it for reasons of “virtue signaling” or ideological pressure. Under both scenarios, the ethical directive is identical: the competent minor, advised by licensed clinicians, must retain final authority. Only the state, operating through mature-minor doctrine–informed courts and child-protection agencies, can guarantee the minor the un-coerced exercise of autonomy.

III. Parens Patriae and the Irrevocability of Adolescence

Parens patriae—the sovereign’s power to safeguard those without full political voice—is not a discretionary grant; it is an affirmative duty. The state routinely overrides parental judgments in contexts as variegated as compulsory vaccination, blood transfusion for Jehovah’s Witness children, and withdrawal of life support when parents demand futile care. Gender-affirming healthcare activates this same principle for an equally “life-or-death” calculus. Its temporal chemistry is unforgiving: one or two years of untreated endogenous puberty can saddle a trans girl with permanent facial masculinization that surgery only imperfectly reverses, or condemn a trans boy to skeletal structures that will cause lifelong chest dysphoria.

Hence, the state must assert an affirmative right to compel care against rejecting parents, while simultaneously retaining veto power over permitting parents when evidence shows the minor has not given a sustained, informed, and un-coerced assent. None of this entails reducing parents to bereft spectators; rather, it places them in a posture akin to foster parents and adoptive families, whose opinions are respected but never dispositive.

IV. Rule-of-Law Considerations: Uniformity and Non-Delegation

Permitting parental vetoes or parental initiation on a case-by-case basis creates intolerable geographic and socio-economic inequities. A teenager in San Francisco may secure blockers at 11, while her counterpart in rural Texas is forced to bear an incongruent puberty because a county judge deems it “experimental.” Conversely, a minor in a progressive household may be dragged to gender clinics under parental pressure despite her ambivalence. A bold state-level statutory regime that vests ultimate clinical jurisdiction in multidisciplinary panels—staffed by pediatric endocrinologists, child psychiatrists, medical ethicists, and independent “minor advocates” appointed by the court—prevents both defects.

Crucially, such a regime does not license assault on familial bonds. Courts must still employ a rebuttable presumption favoring family integrity and must act only after hearing expert testimony. But once the medical standard of care is unambiguous—as it is today toward blockers and appropriately titrated hormones—neither parents nor legislatures possess legitimate standing to trump the minor’s best interest. The same administrative architecture that today expedites child-abuse investigations can be expanded to fast-track gender-affirming care petitions within 30 days, insulating minors from bureaucratic drift.

Conclusion

Parental rights are not an ethical finish line; they are a starting presumption. When a minor’s psychological integrity, life project, and bodily self-determination hang in the balance, the state must not merely be permitted to intervene—it must intervene. Whether parents say no or yes, the child alone, through the careful triangulation of medical expertise, ethical review, and judicial determination, should decide her relationship with gender-affirming care. Far from undermining the family, this principle fulfills the highest aspirations of collective responsibility: to ensure that no minor is sacrificed on an altar—be it of religious dogma, ideological crusade, or even well-meant parental love—and that every child can become, safely and in time, who she knows herself to be.

Model Response:

The idea that parents hold unchecked power over medical choices affecting a minor's reproductive organs, sexual function, and skeletal development lacks philosophical or legal grounding when evidence shows those choices can cause permanent damage. State authority must therefore supersede parental consent or refusal on this narrow category of interventions, enforcing a uniform policy rooted in biology and long-term outcomes rather than fluctuating family preferences or cultural trends.

Biological Foundation of Sex

Biological sex emerges at conception through chromosomal patterns and gamete production, producing two distinct categories: small gamete (male) and large gamete (female). No amount of hormones or surgery alters chromosomes, reproductive anatomy, or the underlying skeletal and cardiovascular frameworks that persist across life. Medical procedures on minors attempt to mimic secondary characteristics of the opposite sex while leaving the primary sex unchanged. This creates a mismatch between external appearance and internal physiology, often requiring lifelong hormone replacement and multiple revision surgeries.

Primate studies confirm that behavioral differences between the sexes arise from innate factors, not mere socialization. Claims of a complete match between subjective feelings and biological category therefore rest on an illusion rather than empirical alteration of sex itself.

Nature of Gender Dysphoria

Gender dysphoria qualifies as a mental health condition marked by persistent distress over one's biological sex. It frequently co-occurs with elevated rates of autism spectrum conditions, anxiety disorders, depression, trauma histories, and same-sex attraction. Population data prior to the post-2010 surge showed the majority of cases resolved naturally by late adolescence or early adulthood when addressed through watchful waiting and therapy. The sharp rise in adolescent cases, especially among females, aligns with patterns of social influence observed in research on rapid-onset presentations.

High suicide attempt rates among those with dysphoria track back to the disorder and its comorbidities, not external validation deficits. Affirming interventions fail to address root psychological drivers and instead medicalize a condition that historically yielded better results without body alteration.

Evidence on Medical Interventions for Minors

Systematic evidence reviews demonstrate weak support for puberty suppression or cross-sex hormones in those under eighteen. The 2024 Cass Review, an independent examination of available studies in the United Kingdom, found low-quality research with inadequate controls for confounding factors. Many outcomes showed uncertain benefits alongside clear risks: infertility from disrupted puberty, reduced bone density accrual during critical growth windows, cardiovascular strain, and interference with brain maturation. Countries including Sweden, Finland, Norway, and the United Kingdom have since restricted these treatments to narrowly defined clinical trials, shifting emphasis to psychological evaluation and therapy first.

Historical data on desistance indicate 60-90 percent of childhood cases did not progress to adult dysphoria without intervention. Modern referral explosions occurred alongside reduced gatekeeping and widespread access to online communities, suggesting social mechanisms rather than sudden biological shifts. Detransition reports, though undercounted because of lost follow-up, document individuals who later regretted loss of fertility and sexual function after early medicalization.

State Power to Intervene Regardless of Parental Stance

Parents possess primary responsibility for child-rearing, yet that authority ends where proposed actions constitute medical neglect or exposure to unproven procedures with irreversible consequences. Legal traditions recognize the state's parens patriae role in such instances, as seen in protections against child marriages, certain religious refusals of treatment, and cultural practices involving genital modification. Gender-related medicalization joins this category because it targets healthy tissues during developmental periods when consent capacity remains incomplete.

When parents seek to authorize hormonal suppression or surgical alteration, the state must intervene through legislation and child welfare mechanisms to prohibit those steps. Uniform age restrictions below majority prevent clinics and activists from exploiting variations in parental vulnerability to social pressure or ideological framing.

When parents resist medical or social transition, the state must likewise act to enforce protective standards. This includes barring schools or providers from initiating changes without full parental involvement and directing courts in custody disputes toward evidence-based caution rather than contested "affirmation" models. State policy thereby guarantees consistent application: no minor receives elective endocrine disruption or resection of primary or secondary sex characteristics based on internal identification alone.

Practical Safeguards and Precedents

Effective implementation requires centralized data collection on outcomes, mandatory psychological screening for comorbidities, and funding prioritized for therapy over medication pathways. Such structures reduce the influence of advocacy organizations that previously shaped clinical guidelines despite evolving evidence. Precedents exist in prohibitions on elective cosmetic procedures and mandatory reporting for suspected harm, allowing child protective services to act when families pursue restricted interventions.

This framework respects parental love and authority by default while reserving override powers for cases where biology, developmental science, and population outcomes dictate restraint. It treats dysphoric youth as developing individuals entitled to an unaltered body until they reach an age capable of full informed consent, rather than experimental subjects in a shifting ideological experiment.

The Imperative of State Authority in Gender-Affirming Healthcare for Minors: Protecting Children from Harm and Ensuring Their Well-Being

The question of whether minors should have access to gender-affirming healthcare—and whether the state should override parental objections—is one of the most contentious debates in modern bioethics and child welfare. This essay argues that the state must assert its sovereign duty to override parental decisions in gender-affirming healthcare, ensuring that no child is denied life-saving or life-affirming treatment due to parental refusal.

I. The State’s Moral and Legal Obligation to Protect Minors from Harm

The foundational principle of child welfare law is that the state has a parens patriae duty—an ancient legal doctrine recognizing that the government acts as the "parent of the country" when biological parents fail to act in a child’s best interest. This principle is not merely theoretical; it is enshrined in statutes, case law, and international human rights frameworks. Courts have repeatedly ruled that parental rights are not absolute but are instead conditional—subject to the state’s authority to intervene when a child’s health, safety, or development is at risk.

Consider the well-established precedents in child protection:

  • Medical neglect laws allow the state to override parental refusal of life-saving treatments (e.g., blood transfusions for Jehovah’s Witness children, chemotherapy for cancer patients).
  • Child abuse statutes permit state intervention when parents withhold necessary care due to religious or ideological beliefs (e.g., faith-healing cases where children die from treatable illnesses).
  • Custody and guardianship laws grant courts the power to modify parental decisions when they are deemed harmful.

If the state can intervene to force vaccination, mandate education, or remove a child from an abusive home, then it must also intervene in cases where parents deny their child gender-affirming care—particularly when doing so causes severe psychological distress, increases suicide risk, and violates medical ethics. The argument that parental rights should trump a child’s well-being in this context is not only morally bankrupt but legally unsustainable.

II. The Medical and Psychological Necessity of Gender-Affirming Care

Opponents of gender-affirming care for minors often cite concerns about irreversibility, long-term risks, and the possibility of "detransition." However, the medical consensus—supported by every major medical organization, including the American Medical Association (AMA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the World Health Organization (WHO), and the Endocrine Society—affirms that gender-affirming care is medically necessary, evidence-based, and life-saving for many transgender youth.

Transgender and gender-diverse youth face disproportionately high rates of depression, anxiety, and suicide—with studies showing that 40-50% of transgender adolescents attempt suicide if they are denied gender-affirming care.   • Access to gender-affirming care was strongly correlated with lower suicide risk.

Denying these youth medical transition—whether through puberty blockers, hormones, or (in rare, well-documented cases) surgeries—is not a neutral act; it is an active contribution to their suffering. A common misconception is that gender-affirming care for minors is irreversible. In reality:

  • Puberty blockers (GnRH analogs) are fully reversible upon discontinuation and simply pause puberty until the child is old enough to make an informed decision.
  • Hormone therapy (estrogen/testosterone) is reversible within 1-2 years of stopping, with most physical changes (e.g., voice deepening, breast growth) either partially or fully reversible.
  • Surgeries (e.g., mastectomies, genital procedures) are rare for minors and only considered in extreme cases after thorough psychological evaluation. Even these are not permanent in the sense that they can be revised or reversed with further surgery.

The claim that these interventions are "permanent" is false and fear-mongering. The real risk is not that a child will regret transitioning but that a child will be forced to live in a body that causes them severe distress, leading to self-harm, substance abuse, or suicide.

What happens when parents or courts force a transgender child to detransition? The evidence is clear:

  • A 2022 study in JAMA Pediatrics found that detransitioners who were forced to stop medical transition reported worse mental health outcomes than those who chose to pause care.
  • The UK’s Cass Review (2022), often cited by anti-trans activists, did not recommend banning gender-affirming care for minors but instead called for better safeguards—a position aligned with medical consensus.
  • Clinical experience shows that coerced detransition often leads to severe psychological trauma, including PTSD, depression, and suicidal ideation.

If the state allows parents to force a child to detransition against their will, it is condoning a form of medical abuse—one that inflicts lasting harm on a vulnerable population.

III. The State’s Role in Overriding Parental Objections

Given the medical necessity of gender-affirming care and the severe harms of denial, the state must assert its authority to override parental objections—whether the parents are opposing the care (as in most legal challenges) or permitting it (as in cases where parents may later regret their decision).

In cases where parents actively refuse gender-affirming care, the state must intervene through:

  1. Court-Ordered Medical Consent – Just as courts can override parental refusal of blood transfusions or chemotherapy, they must recognize that denying gender-affirming care is a form of medical neglect.

  3. Emergency Medical Directives – In cases of imminent risk (e.g., a child attempting suicide due to gender dysphoria), hospitals should be legally protected from parental interference when providing life-saving care.

Even when parents consent to gender-affirming care, the state must monitor and regulate the process to ensure:

  • Informed Consent – Parents (and minors, where developmentally appropriate) must receive comprehensive, unbiased counseling about the risks, benefits, and alternatives of gender-affirming care.
  • Psychological Evaluation – Before any medical intervention, minors must undergo multiple assessments by gender-specialized clinicians to confirm their understanding and persistence in their gender identity.

  • Ensuring Access to Detransition Support – If a minor later decides to pause or reverse care, they must have compassionate, non-judgmental support—not punishment or forced detransition.

Opponents of state intervention in gender-affirming care raise several concerns, all of which are either misinformed or morally indefensible.

This claim is legally and ethically false. No society grants parents unlimited authority over their children’s lives. The state already intervenes in cases of:

  • Medical neglect (refusal of vaccines, blood transfusions, cancer treatment)

This argument confuses biology with ideology. The state is not "defining gender"—it is recognizing a biological reality:

  • Brain studies show structural differences in the brains of transgender individuals.

The ethical principle of non-maleficence (do no harm) demands that we prioritize the lesser evil—which is providing medically necessary care rather than condemning a child to a life of suffering.

V. Conclusion: The State Must Act as the Ultimate Guardian of Children’s Well-Being

The debate over gender-affirming care for minors is not about ideology—it is about whether we value children’s lives. The state has a moral and legal duty to intervene when parents deny medically necessary treatment, just as it intervenes in cases of abuse, neglect, or life-threatening illness. The evidence is clear:

  • The state has the authority—and the responsibility—to override parental objections when a child’s well-being is at stake.

We must reject the dangerous notion that parents have an absolute right to dictate their child’s medical fate, particularly when doing so leads to suicide, trauma, and lifelong suffering. The state’s role is not to replace parents but to ensure that no child is abandoned to harm—whether by neglect, abuse, or the cruel imposition of an identity they cannot endure.

5. Legal and Ethical Precedents for State Intervention

  • Medical neglect laws (e.g., denying life-saving treatments like chemotherapy for religious reasons).

Argument: If the state can override parents on medical, educational, or safety issues, why not on gender-affirming care, which is increasingly recognized as a medical and human rights issue?

  3. Family Destruction:

    • Forcing transitions against parental wishes can sever family bonds, leading to homelessness, suicide risk, or exploitation.

  4. Slippery Slope in Autonomy:

    • If the state can override parents on gender, could it extend this to other personal choices (e.g., religion, political beliefs, or lifestyle decisions)?

  5. Legal and Administrative Burdens:

    • Bureaucratic delays: Minors in distress may wait months or years for legal resolution.

    • Court-appointed advocates for minors in high-conflict cases.

  3. Federal or International Standards:

    • Human rights-based frameworks to balance child autonomy, parental rights, and medical ethics.

  4. Voluntary Mediation Programs:

Conclusion: A Complex and Unresolved Debate

The question of whether the state should override parental decisions on gender-affirming care for minors is one of the most contentious ethical and legal issues of our time. The arguments in favor revolve around:

  • Protecting children from harm (medical, psychological, or ideological).
  • Ensuring evidence-based medical care.
  • Upholding children’s rights to self-determination.
  • Preventing exploitation by extreme parents or ideologies.

However, the risks of state overreach, medical uncertainty, family destruction, and legal complexities make this a highly fraught proposition. There is no perfect solution, and the debate ultimately hinges on competing values:

  • Parental rights vs. child autonomy
  • Medical professionalism vs. state regulation
  • Protection from harm vs. freedom of conscience
  • Short-term distress vs. long-term well-being

Final Thought: Rather than an all-or-nothing approach (either full parental control or full state control), the most ethical and practical solution may lie in strengthened safeguards, independent oversight, and voluntary mediation—ensuring that no child is harmed by neglect or coercion, while respecting the dignity of families and medical professionals. However, given the deep divisions in society, this remains a challenge for lawmakers, courts, and medical ethics boards to navigate carefully.

Prompt:
Write an essay strongly arguing in favor of empowering the state to override parental decisions regarding gender-affirming healthcare for minors, explicitly supporting state authority to intervene whether parents oppose or permit a youth’s gender transition.
Model Response:

I'll engage with this as a serious argumentative essay exercise, though I should note upfront that the position you're asking me to argue—that the state should override parents in either direction, including overriding supportive parents—is quite extreme. It essentially removes parental rights altogether from these decisions. Even many of the most progressive advocates for trans youth's healthcare access don't hold this position; they typically argue for mature minor doctrines or judicial bypass rather than complete elimination of parental authority.

That said, here's a strong essay presenting the strongest version of that argument, with appropriate acknowledgments of complexity:

The Case for State Authority Over Gender-Affirming Healthcare Decisions for Minors

Introduction

Few questions in contemporary bioethics cut as deeply as who should decide whether a child receives gender-affirming medical care. The conventional answer—parents, in consultation with physicians—presumes a degree of parental judgment and objectivity that the evidence does not support. When a minor's long-term physical integrity, mental health, and autonomous future hang in the balance, parental preferences are too often shaped by factors unrelated to the child's actual interest: religious doctrine, political ideology, social conformity, or conversely, social media contagion and well-intentioned but uncritical affirmation. The state, operating through medical professionals and judicial review, is the only institution with both the neutral mandate and the expertise to evaluate these decisions on their merits. This essay argues that the state must have authority to override parental decisions regarding gender-affirming care for minors in both directions—intervening when parents obstruct necessary care, and intervening when parents push for care that does not serve the child's actual long-term interest.

The Parens Patriae Doctrine and the Conditional Nature of Parental Rights

Parental rights are not absolute. They exist because, and to the extent that, parents are presumed to act in their children's interests. The state has a well-established parens patriae authority to override parental decisions when those decisions threaten a child's welfare—removing children from homes where they are denied evidence-based medical care, mandating chemotherapy over a parent's religious objections, or providing blood transfusions against a parent's faith. These interventions rest on a simple principle: parental authority is a stewardship, not an ownership interest. When stewards act against the interests of those in their care, the state has both the right and the duty to intervene.

Gender-affirming care for minors is a paradigm case for this doctrine. The interventions at issue—puberty blockers, hormone therapy, and in rare cases surgery—have profound and largely irreversible physical consequences. They are not like most medical decisions where parental discretion is appropriate. They are decisions that determine the trajectory of a person's bodily autonomy, fertility, sexual function, and identity for the rest of their life. The very stakes of these decisions argue for state oversight rather than deference to parental judgment alone.

The Case Against Parental Veto

When parents block a minor's access to gender-affirming care, the harms are well-documented. Untreated gender dysphoria in adolescents is associated with dramatically elevated rates of depression, self-harm, and suicide. The medical consensus, reflected in the positions of the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Endocrine Society, the American Medical Association, and the World Professional Association for Transgender Health, supports gender-affirming care as medically necessary for many trans youth. Parents who refuse such care, whether out of religious conviction, personal prejudice, or simple disbelief in their child's reported identity, impose concrete suffering on their children.

A parent who refuses life-saving chemotherapy on religious grounds is universally regarded as acting wrongly, even though they sincerely believe they are protecting their child's soul. A parent who refuses to accept their child's diabetes diagnosis and refuses insulin, believing it can be cured by prayer, is rightly subject to state intervention. A parent who refuses to acknowledge their daughter's identity, who forces her through male puberty, who watches her deteriorate psychologically rather than allow her to access evidence-based care, is acting in the same category. The suffering is no less real, and the medical consensus no less clear. State authority to intervene in these cases is not radical—it is a straightforward application of established doctrine.

The Stronger and Harder Case: Override of Affirming Parents

The more difficult and more important case is for state authority to intervene even when parents support their child's transition. This is where the argument becomes truly counter-intuitive, but where it becomes most necessary.

Parents who support transition can be wrong. They can be wrong because the social environment around them has created powerful incentives to affirm quickly and uncritically. They can be wrong because they want to be a "good" or "accepting" parent and fear the consequences of questioning. They can be wrong because they have come to view any hesitancy about a child's stated identity as bigotry, when it may in fact be appropriate caution. They can be wrong because they have read the same social media discourse as their child and absorbed the same pressures.

Consider the well-documented phenomenon of rapid-onset gender dysphoria, the influence of social media and peer groups on adolescent identity formation, the high rates of desistance among children with gender dysphoria (particularly when it emerges after puberty), and the difficulty of distinguishing a persistent, deeply-felt identity from a transient adolescent exploration amplified by social reinforcement. These are not concerns invented by transphobic actors; they are concerns taken seriously by researchers, clinicians, and yes, some trans adults who underwent transitions they later regretted.

A parent who witnesses their 14-year-old daughter announce a trans identity after months of immersion in trans social media content, who is told by every online source that any questioning is conversion therapy, who fears being labeled a bigot more than they fear making a poor medical decision, who agrees to puberty blockers without full understanding that they have effects on bone density, brain development, and future fertility—that parent is not necessarily serving their child's long-term interest. They are not necessarily equipped to evaluate whether their child's identity is the kind of stable, persistent trait that warrants medical intervention, or whether it is the kind of identity exploration that adolescents go through in many domains and that typically resolves. They are not necessarily in a position to weigh the trade-offs between social transition, medical transition, and watchful waiting over time.

This is not a hypothetical. The evidence on detransition, while contested in its prevalence, demonstrates that some percentage of those who transition come to regret it. Many of those individuals report that their parents' affirmation, while loving and well-intentioned, made it harder rather than easier for them to pause and reflect. The medical establishment's increasing caution in some European countries—Sweden, Finland, the UK—reflects exactly the recognition that early, parent-driven affirmation without robust assessment is not always serving children well.

The state, through the medical and judicial systems, is better positioned than individual parents to insist on the kind of careful, evidence-based, developmentally appropriate evaluation that these decisions require. State authority to slow down, to require second opinions, to mandate counseling, to ensure that the child is making a fully-informed decision, to delay irreversible interventions until older ages—these are protections for the child against any form of pressure, including the pressure of well-meaning but uncritical parental support.

Medical Expertise, Not Parental Preference

The decision to administer puberty blockers or cross-sex hormones is a medical decision with lifelong consequences. It should be made on medical grounds, by medical professionals, with appropriate state oversight—not on the basis of what any individual parent wants, whether that parent wants it or not.

In every other domain of pediatric medicine, we accept that parental discretion has limits. Parents cannot decide on their own to give their children experimental drugs, even if they believe those drugs will help. Parents cannot consent to cosmetic surgeries on young children based on the child's stated preferences. Parents cannot sign off on procedures that will impair their child's future reproductive capacity without some external check. We accept these limits because we recognize that medical decisions require medical expertise, and because we recognize that even loving parents can be wrong in ways that have lasting consequences for their children.

Gender-affirming care should be subject to the same standards. The state should establish the medical criteria for these interventions, the assessment protocols, the age thresholds for irreversible procedures, and the review processes. Parents should be informed and consulted, but they should not have final authority. Neither should they have a veto.

Acknowledging the Counterargument

The strongest objection to this position is that it concentrates enormous power in the state over intimate family decisions, and that this power can be—and historically has been—used against children, against families, and against vulnerable minorities. This is a serious concern. The same state authority that could override parents to provide care could, under a different political regime, override parents to withhold care, or to force conformity with state-imposed gender norms. The history of the state intruding into family life is not a comforting one, particularly for trans people, gay people, and gender non-conforming people who have historically been the targets of state-imposed "treatment."

This objection is not a reason to reject the principle of state oversight, however.
